schools.summary: Ellicott: the accession notice stands word for word as 2 Kings 15:33 (only the name Jotham added); Jerushah daughter of Zadok perhaps the high priest of 1 Chron. 6:12 (cf. 2 Chron. 22:11).
Gill passes over the bare regnal figures as matter already told, deferring to the parallel.
Clarke sketches the whole arc of the reign: Jotham succeeds Uzziah and reigns well, builds, wages successful wars, dies — an almost wholly favourable reign.
Gill notes only that he did that which was right, as the parallel said.

Keil reads the temple-reservation as marking a son who did not repeat Uzziah's presumption; Ellicott explains the chronicler adds it because he alone recorded the sacrilege, and reads 'did yet corruptly' as a paraphrase of 2 Kings 15:35 (cf. Micah 3:10-12; Hosea 4:1-2).
Clarke: Jotham copied his father so far as it was constitutional and avoided the sacrilege of 2 Chron. 26:16; Wesley: imitate the esteemed only so far as they do well.
Henry half-turns the people's corruption back on the king (perhaps wanting in reforming zeal), yet lays the blame on a people who under a good king would not be good.

themes: imitating the good only in their good

schools.summary: Gill marks simply that he built the high gate of the house of the LORD.

Ellicott presses the emphatic pronoun, reads the 'high' as the upper/northern gate (Ezek. 9:2; the holy quarter, Isa. 14:13, Ps. 48:2), and traces the Ophel detail to a good ancient source ('much'=larob, a favourite word); Keil calls the upper gate the only work Kings records and sets the Ophel wall connecting Zion to Moriah (2 Chron. 26:9).
Clarke, with the Targum, takes Ophel for the most pregnable part of the wall, specially fortified; Wesley: 'built' means repaired, for the gate stood before.

themes: the upper gate of the temple

schools.summary: Gill sets the cities in the mountainous hill country of Judea.

Keil reads the work as continuing Uzziah's building for the herds (2 Chron. 26:10); Ellicott fixes 'castles' (biraniyoth, as at 2 Chron. 17:12) but warns that the prophets denounced trust in fenced cities as treason against Jehovah the true fortress (Hosea 8:14; Isa. 2:15; 17:3-4).
Clarke: the castles and towers were built to protect the country people against marauders.

outliers.note: Alone sounds the prophetic caution that confidence in fenced cities was denounced as a kind of treason against Jehovah, the people's true shield and fortress.

themes: castles and towers in the forests
protection of herds and country folk
the prophets against trust in walls

schools.summary: Gill sets the war in its long frame: Ammon subdued by David, restless in Jehoshaphat's day, resisting again under Jotham but failing.

Keil: Ammon, tributary to Uzziah, refused after his death and was re-subdued, paying 100 talents of silver and grain for three years then lapsing; Ellicott fixes the kor measure (1 Kings 4:22; 2 Chron. 2:10) and ties the lapse to the Syro-Ephraite war (2 Kings 15:37).
Clarke doubts whether the tribute simply followed the victory; some hold Ammon paid three years, revolted, and were then utterly subdued.

debates.question: Did the three-year Ammonite tribute follow Jotham's victory, or did the conquest follow the tribute?

sides.position: Jotham defeated Ammon and imposed the tribute, which they paid three years before falling away
It is not evident the tribute resulted from the victory; some hold Ammon paid three years, revolted, and were then utterly subdued

schools.summary: Gill reads the might from the acts told: towers, castles, fortified cities, conquered enemies.

Keil presses past the works to the ground: Jotham strengthened himself because he walked steadfastly before Jahve, not incurring guilt as Uzziah did (2 Chron. 26:16), and doubts the Rezin/Pekah war (2 Kings 15:37) belongs among 'all his wars'; Ellicott parses 'became mighty'=strengthened himself (2 Chron. 13:21) and 'prepared his ways'=directed them (Prov. 21:29; cf. 2 Chron. 12:14; 20:33; 1 Chron. 12:17; 1 Sam. 7:3; Gen. 17:1) as the writer's moral reflection.
Henry draws the maxim: the more steadfast in religion, the mightier to resist evil and do good.
Gill reads 'all his wars' widely — with Syrians and the ten tribes as well as Ammon.

Ellicott marks the chronicler varying Kings' 'all that he did' (2 Kings 15:36) to 'all his wars and his ways' to hint at the Syro-Ephraite war (2 Kings 15:37); Keil hears in the phrase a fuller military record and frames it before the death-formula.
Clarke: in his days Rezin and Pekah began to cut Judah short (2 Kings 15:37); the fuller histories are lost, both records abridged; Jotham's was the last politically prosperous reign before the ruin.

themes: the varied phrase hinting at war

schools.summary: Gill registers only that the regnal figures are here repeated as before.

Ellicott and Keil agree the doubled accession-formula (a word-for-word repetition of 2 Kings 15:33, dropping the queen-mother clause) is best explained by two authorities, one placing the notice at the reign's start and another at its end — a visible seam of the chronicler's method.
Keil gives the plain sense: Jotham died as his fathers died, was buried honourably in the city of David with no note of dishonour, and Ahaz his son succeeded.
Clarke sets the death at the hinge of history — the last politically prosperous reign, after which Judah continued to be cut short until wholly ruined.
Henry: the LORD often removes wise and pious rulers and sends others whose vices punish a people that valued not their mercies — fulfilled at once in Ahaz.

themes: a pious ruler removed in judgment
